q: The empirical relative error scales as ~0.093 * delta^2 on our depth-4 T=30 tree, but Lemma 5 only guarantees the O(delta) envelope [(1-delta)T, (1+delta)T]. Is this delta^2 behavior generic across all trees, or is it a special property of complete binary trees / our particular starting state overlap?
basis: Direct observation: relative error dropped by exactly ~4x each time delta halved across a 200x range of delta in scaling_test.py, giving log-log slope 2.00. Paper's Lemma 5 does not state this tighter O(delta^2) bound.
next_steps: Sweep delta on random branching-factor trees (Galton-Watson trees) and on deep skinny trees; if the delta^2 scaling persists, look at Sections 6.5-6.8 to see if a sharper bound can be proved from the discriminant matrix analysis.

q: Our measured phase-gap constant factor was 0.421, uniformly ~0.7% below the naive prediction 2*delta/sqrt(2) = 0.424 across depths 1-7. Is there a subleading correction of the form theta_min = 2*delta/sqrt(2nT) * (1 - c(n)/sqrt(T)) hiding in the discriminant matrix analysis?
basis: The 'measured/theory' ratio in quadratic_speedup.json is monotone increasing with depth (0.9926 -> 0.9970) but never crosses 1, suggesting a finite-size correction that vanishes as T -> infinity.
next_steps: Compute the exact analytic form of theta_min for complete binary trees at fixed depth (the discriminant matrix K has enough symmetry to yield a closed form) and compare to our numeric result at 10 significant digits.

q: Algorithm 1 requires knowing an upper bound n on the tree depth to set alpha = sqrt(2n)/delta. How badly does the estimator degrade when n_guess >> n_true (over-estimated depth), and can the paper's guarantee be salvaged by any adaptive alpha-doubling scheme?
basis: Neither the Theorem 2 statement nor the Lemma 5 proof appears to give a graceful-degradation clause for a mis-calibrated n. In practice a caller often knows only a loose upper bound.
next_steps: Run Algorithm 1 on a fixed T=30 tree with n_guess = {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64} keeping delta=0.3; measure how the Lemma 5 window is violated (or not) as n_guess grows.

q: The estimator bias is one-sided in all our runs: hat T > T for every tree we tested. Is this a fundamental artifact of the identity T = 1/(alpha^2 sin^2(theta/2)) (Jensen convexity of 1/sin^2 gives an upward bias), and if so can a simple correction term like hat T -> hat T - c/alpha^2 restore approximate unbiasedness without additional queries?
basis: All 8 instances in results_algorithm1.json satisfy hat T > T; the smallest overestimate is +0.6% (ternary depth-3, T=39 -> hat T=39.24) and the largest is +2.3% (complete binary depth-1, T=2 -> hat T=2.045).
next_steps: Prove (or disprove) that E[1/(alpha^2 sin^2(theta_hat/2))] > T under the paper's assumptions on the eigenvalue estimation output, then propose a debiasing correction and measure its effect empirically.

q: The direct-sum construction R_A = ⊕_{v in V_A} D_v relies on V_A being an independent set (which holds for trees by bipartition). Theorem 2 claims the same algorithm works for arbitrary DAGs, yet in a genuine DAG two even-distance vertices CAN share an edge. What is the minimal DAG structure that breaks the direct-sum trick, and what structural condition beyond acyclicity is actually needed for correctness?
basis: The paper's Lemma 3 asserts R_A and R_B can be implemented by direct sums of diffusions Dv, but the proof (and our own construction) relies on H_v subspaces being pairwise orthogonal within V_A / V_B. This is not automatic for DAGs.
next_steps: Construct a small DAG with two even-distance vertices sharing an edge (e.g. diamond graph with 4 vertices), attempt to build R_A as-is, and check whether the resulting operator is still unitary and satisfies Lemmas 4 and 5. If not, identify the minimal structural condition (e.g. 'the even-parity subgraph is edge-disjoint from the odd-parity subgraph') that saves the algorithm.
